To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
concrete and abstract multiword processing relies on different brain regions, and that concrete and abstract words are represented differently in the brain.
the neural representation of both concrete and purely abstract language is grounded in the sensorimotor cortex, but that abstract language is represented in a different way than concrete language.

concrete and abstract multi-words are represented in the brain in a continuum of neural activation, and that the neural network of action representation is involved in both concrete and non-concrete language comprehension.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how abstract language content is represented.
the neural representation of abstract language and the role of the sensorimotorsystem.
a new perspective on the embodied cognition of abstract concepts and language.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
abstract words are not embodied in the same sense as concrete words.
abstract words have no sensorimotor representation and are not grounded in the sensorimotor cortex, but that they are represented in a different way than concrete words.
abstract words do not have an embodied representation, but that abstract words can be represented by a combination of different cognitive processes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
abstract words are not completely devoid of embodied properties.
abstract words are represented by a combination of the linguistic and sensorimotor neural systems, but to different degrees depending on the degree of concreteness of the abstract words.
abstract language content is grounded in sensorimotor representations, but to a lesser extent than concrete content, while concrete language content is more dependent on the linguistic system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
concrete and abstract multi-words are processed differently.
concrete and abstract language is represented in the brain in terms of a continuum of activation of the sensorimotorsystem and the linguistic system.

the neural representation of abstract language content is grounded in sensorimotor properties, and that the neural representation is modulated by the linguistic properties of the multi-word expressions.
